title: Consistency Models
summary: The spectrum from strong to eventual consistency, and the session guarantees users actually notice.

slides.markdown:
Every distributed database has to answer one question: after a write, what does a read see, and when? **Consistency models** are the menu of answers, and they form a spectrum — the strongest guarantees cost the most latency and availability, the weakest cost the most confusion.

Think of a group chat over a shaky connection: your message sent, but not everyone sees it in the same order at the same instant. This topic gives you the vocabulary — strong, eventual, causal — to reason about what a system actually promises and what a user will notice when it doesn't.

slides.sectionTitle: The consistency spectrum: strong to eventual
slides.markdown:
Consistency models sit on a spectrum, not a binary switch. At one end, **strong consistency** guarantees every read sees the most recent write, as if there were only one copy of the data. At the other, **eventual consistency** only guarantees that replicas converge *if writes stop* — with no promise about when a given read catches up.

Between them sit intermediate models — causal consistency, read-your-writes, monotonic reads — that give specific, useful guarantees without paying for full strong consistency.

The interview move: name where a system sits on this spectrum and why, rather than treating "consistent" as one fixed thing.

slides.sectionTitle: Strong consistency: what it guarantees and what it costs
slides.markdown:
**Strong consistency** (often linearizability) means every read reflects the latest completed write, and all clients agree on the order of operations — the system behaves as if it were a single machine, even though it's replicated.

That guarantee is expensive: a write typically can't be acknowledged until enough replicas confirm it, and a network partition forces a choice — refuse the read/write (stay consistent) or answer with possibly-stale data (stay available). That's the CAP trade-off in practice.

Use strong consistency where being wrong is worse than being slow: account balances, inventory counts, anything where two people can't both "win".

slides.sectionTitle: Eventual consistency: what "eventual" actually means in practice
slides.markdown:
**Eventual consistency** promises that if no new writes arrive, all replicas will *eventually* converge to the same value — it says nothing about how long that takes. In practice "eventually" is usually milliseconds to seconds, but under replication lag, network issues, or high write volume it can stretch to minutes.

This is the trade for availability and low latency: a replica can answer a read immediately from whatever it has locally, even if that's not the newest write.

It fits data where a stale read is a minor inconvenience, not a correctness bug: a social media like count, a product view counter, a friend's "last seen" timestamp.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a write propagating to replicas over time
slides.markdown:
![Timeline of a write reaching replicas at different times, with a stale read in between](assets/write-propagation-timeline.svg)

A write doesn't reach every replica at the same instant — it lands on one node first, then propagates. A read that hits a replica before the write arrives there sees the old value, even though the write already "happened" elsewhere.

This is the entire eventual-consistency story in one picture: convergence is guaranteed, timing isn't. The gap between write and full propagation is exactly the window where staleness is possible.

slides.sectionTitle: Causal consistency and session guarantees: read-your-writes, monotonic reads
slides.markdown:
**Causal consistency** guarantees that operations with a cause-and-effect relationship are seen in that order by everyone — if you post a comment replying to a question, no one sees the reply before the question. It doesn't order unrelated writes at all, which is what makes it cheaper than strong consistency.

Two practical session guarantees fall out of this idea. **Read-your-writes**: after you write something, your own subsequent reads see it (no reading a stale replica right after posting). **Monotonic reads**: once you've seen a value, you never see an older one on a later read, even if a later request lands on a different replica.

Most "eventually consistent but doesn't feel broken" products are quietly relying on these two guarantees.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: consistency models by what a user can observe
slides.markdown:
The clearest way to compare models is by what a user could notice going wrong.

| Model | A user could see... | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Strong | Nothing stale, ever — always the latest write | Highest latency, availability trade-off under partition |
| Causal | Unrelated updates out of order, but never effect-before-cause | Moderate — needs to track dependencies |
| Read-your-writes | Other people's updates late, but never their own edits missing | Low — track per-session writes |
| Eventual | Any stale value, for an unbounded time, from anyone | Lowest latency, highest availability |

**How to decide:** ask what a user would actually notice if the guarantee were dropped — if the honest answer is "nothing they'd complain about," eventual consistency is probably enough.

**Wrong belief:** "It's eventually consistent, so replicas will catch up almost instantly — I don't need to design around staleness."

**Why it's wrong:** "eventual" has no time bound. Under normal load it might be milliseconds, but a slow replica, a network blip, or a replication backlog can stretch that to seconds or minutes — and the system gives no signal to the client about which case it's in.

**Correct model:** if a user-visible flow depends on seeing their own recent write (a profile edit, a posted comment), don't assume eventual consistency will feel instant — either read from the primary for that specific case, or design the UI to tolerate a visible lag.
